about: Dofras (Dover): the minster in the Roman fort and the short crossing, 793-1066. Written 6 Oct 2026 from Design/content/dossiers/dofras.md and the spine. A draft for the user to overwrite. Woven with the other ports of the region on 7 Oct 2026: ties answered both ways with Sarre, Fordwic, Lundenwic and Hamwic, beats added there and at Gipeswic and Dommoc (the pilgrims' bundles, the lighthouse riddle, the long song), and the region's cards (Data/encounters/england_south_east_793.json) hung on the sites and the beats.

ports.summary: A minster town in a gap of the white cliffs, where a short chalk stream called the Dour runs out over shingle: timber houses and Saint Martin's wooden church stand inside the walls of a Roman fort, and on each height above them is an old Roman light tower with no fire in it. In 793 it answers to King Offa of Mercia through a reeve, and half the toll of the landing belongs to the clerks of Saint Martin. A merchant comes for the crossing, the shortest there is to the Franks, for Kentish cloth and wool, and for news, because whoever is going over the water or coming back has to wait here for the wind.
ports.seasons: The crossing runs most of the year, and the other shore shows as a pale line on a clear day. Wool comes down at midsummer, pilgrims wait on the shingle from Pentecost to Michaelmas, the herring boats go out from Michaelmas to Saint Andrew, and the town keeps its own feast at Martinmas in slaughter month, when the beasts that cannot be wintered are killed and salted. A winter gale from the south-west shuts the strand for days and heaps the shingle across the stream mouth.

history.text: The Romans build a shore fort at Dubris, 'the waters', beside the older harbour and its two light towers on the heights. The English houses of the game's years stand inside its walls.
history.source: Wikipedia (en) 'Dubris'; Kent Archaeological Rescue Unit, B. Philp, The Discovery and Excavation of Anglo-Saxon Dover (2003), as listed at karu.org.uk. The date is about 270.

history.text: By the tradition of the house, King Eadbald of Kent, who died this year, set twenty-two canons in Saint Mary's chapel on the hill.
history.source: Victoria County History, Kent, vol. 2, 'The priory of Dover' (from the priory's late registers: a tradition, not a record)

history.text: King Wihtred's law for the men of Kent: the church pays no tax and prays for the king; there are penalties for gifts to idols and for meat in a fast; a stranger who leaves the track and neither shouts nor blows his horn may be taken for a thief.
history.source: The laws of Wihtred, 6 September 695: Wikipedia (en) 'Law of Wihtred'

history.text: By the same tradition King Wihtred moves the canons down from the hill to a new church of Saint Martin in the town, built to keep a vow to the saint, and gives them half the toll of the port. Hasted gives the year as 691.
history.source: Victoria County History, Kent, vol. 2; E. Hasted, History of Kent vol. 9 (1800); Wikipedia (en) 'Dover Priory' (house tradition)

history.text: King Offa dies on 29 July. Eadberht Praen takes the kingdom of Kent, and Archbishop Æthelheard, Offa's man, leaves Canterbury. Where he took ship is not recorded.
history.source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 794 for 796; Alcuin's letters of 796-797; chronicle_793.json 796-summer-eadberht-kent

history.text: Cenwulf of Mercia lays Kent waste, takes Eadberht Praen and maims him, and sets his own brother Cuthred over the Kentish.
history.source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 796 for 798; chronicle_793.json 798-kent-ravaged

history.text: King Cuthred dies and Cenwulf rules Kent himself.
history.source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 805 for 807; chronicle_793.json 807-cuthred-kent

history.text: The emperor Charles has the old light tower at Boulogne repaired and a fire lit on it at night. From the heights of Dofras it can be seen. The towers here stay dark.
history.source: Annales regni Francorum 811 (chronicle_793.json 811-10-boulogne-lighthouse). That it was seen from Dover is the game's: the strait is 33 km at its narrowest (Wikipedia en 'Strait of Dover') (?). No source says either Dover tower was lit after the Romans.

history.text: After the fight at Ellendun the men of Kent turn to Ecgberht of Wessex, and the reeve at Dofras is a West Saxon king's man.
history.source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 823 for 825; Research/thames_mouth_c800_notes.md

history.text: The heathen men winter on Thanet for the first time, and three hundred and fifty ships come into the Thames mouth and storm Canterbury. Nothing is recorded of Dofras.
history.source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 851 (Giles 1847); chronicle_793.json

history.text: At some time in this century Saint Martin's church burns and is built again in timber on the same lines. No cause is recorded, and no year: the game sets it here.
history.source: The Dover Historian, 'St Martin-le-Grand' (2014), reporting the Kent Archaeological Rescue Unit's dig; the year is the game's (?)

history.text: The heathen army sits on Thanet and takes the Kentish men's promise of silver, then steals away by night and overruns all east Kent.
history.source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 865 (Giles 1847)

history.text: The great army crosses from Boulogne in two hundred and fifty ships, horses and all, and goes up the Limen to Appledore. The whole fleet passes through the strait.
history.source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 893 for 892 (Giles 1847); chronicle_793.json

history.text: By about this time pennies are struck at Dofras with the town's name on them.
history.source: Dover Museum, 'Saxon Dover' (a mint by the middle of the 10th century). The first may be King Æthelstan's, 924-939 (?).

history.text: Olaf comes with ninety-three ships to Folkestone and harries it, and goes on to Sandwich. Dofras is not named.
history.source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle (A) 993 for 991; chronicle_793.json 991-08-maldon; realms/england_south.md (the table's listing of dofras is corrected there)

history.text: About now a church of Saint Mary is built on the east height of flint and Roman tile, cross-shaped with a tower in the middle, and the Roman light tower beside it is given a fifth stage and bells.
history.source: Wikipedia (en) 'St Mary in Castro, Dover'; Dover Museum, 'St Mary in Castro'

history.text: Thorkell's army lands at Sandwich after Lammas, and the people of east Kent buy peace of it for three thousand pounds.
history.source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 1009 (Giles 1847); chronicle_793.json

history.text: Count Eustace of Boulogne's men put on their mail short of the town and demand lodging where they please. A householder is wounded, kills his man and is killed at his own hearth; more than twenty townsmen die and nineteen of the Frenchmen. The king orders Earl Godwine to harry Dofras. He will not, and is driven out of England.
history.source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle (E) 1048 for 1051 and (D) 1052 for 1051, Avalon Project (Ingram 1823 and Giles 1847 (?)); Wikipedia (en) 'Eustace II, Count of Boulogne'

history.text: Godwine and Harold come back by sea, and at Dofras and the other harbours take as many ships and hostages as they choose before sailing on to London.
history.source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle (E) 1052, Avalon Project

history.text: In October Duke William comes from Hastings. While the people are yielding his men set fire to the stronghold, and the town burns with it, Saint Martin's among the rest. He stays eight days adding to the defences.
history.source: Dover Museum, 'Norman Dover' (from William of Poitiers); Domesday Book in Hasted's translation (1800): 'on his first arrival in England, the town itself was burnt'

eras.text: Offa's Kent. A reeve who is the Mercian king's man takes the king's half of the toll and a clerk of Saint Martin takes the other. The Frankish shore is shut to English merchants by King Charles's order, so the shingle is full of people who say they are pilgrims, and the boatmen of the strand have never been busier. It is a hungry year and the minster feeds a line at its door.

Kent rises under Eadberht Praen and is beaten flat in 798; the reeve changes, and changes again. The peace of the two kings holds over the water, pilgrims cross free and traders pay, and after 811 a fire can be seen at night on the far shore where the emperor has lit the tower of Boulogne. Dofras stays dark.

West Saxon Kent. The same houses, the same clerks, a king's reeve with a different accent. Quentovic over the water is at its fullest and the crossing is steady work: wool and cloth out, wine, querns and pots back.

The heathen years. Fleets winter on Thanet and Sheppey and pass through the strait in hundreds; a watch is kept on the east height and people drive their beasts inland when the word comes. Saint Martin's burns and is built again. The landing over the water thins, and fewer cross.

The kings of Wessex hold all England. Pennies are struck here with the town's name, the canons' church is in its fourth timber building, and the men of the strand go north each autumn after the herring. Quentovic is a name on old coin; boats cross to Boulogne and to the bank under Montreuil.

The fleets come back. Folkestone is harried in 991, Thorkell lands at Sandwich in 1009 and east Kent pays three thousand pounds for a peace that lasts a season. A stone church of Saint Mary goes up on the height and bells hang in the old light tower. Under Cnut there is one king on both shores of the sea, and nobody is afraid of a sail.

King Edward's time: a town of burgesses with a hall of their own, who owe the king twenty ships for fifteen days in the year and carry his messengers over to Wissant, and are quit of toll through all England for it. The king's peace lies on the town from Michaelmas to Saint Andrew. In 1051 they fight Count Eustace's men in their own doorways. In October 1066 the town burns.

sites.name: The shingle in the stream mouth
sites.see: A grey shingle bank across the mouth of a clear chalk stream, and white cliffs going up on either hand. In front, small clinker boats lie hauled above the weed line on rollers with their oars lashed inboard; a keel sits on the stones at the ebb with planks down to the pebbles. Behind, the stream widens into a tidal pool under the old fort wall. Shingle growls in the backwash, gulls quarrel over fish guts, and on a clear morning the far shore is a pale line.
sites.source: Where boats lay is not recorded: the Roman harbour was the Dour's estuary, and shingle kept closing its mouth (Wikipedia en 'Port of Dover', 'River Dour'); Hasted (1800) has the haven still 'much further within land' at the Conquest. The beach is the guess of ports_793.json. The far shore seen on a clear day: Wikipedia (en) 'Strait of Dover'.

sites.name: The two tallies, at the old south gate
sites.see: A gap in a Roman wall of flint and red tile, twice a man's height and furred with ivy, where the path from the shingle comes in. A lean-to of planks stands against a round bastion; under it are a bench, a balance and two bundles of notched sticks hung on separate pegs. The reeve's man sits at one end of the bench and a tonsured clerk at the other, and each watches the other count.
sites.source: The canons held 'a moiety of the toll of the port', by their tradition from Wihtred (Victoria County History, Kent, vol. 2); Domesday gives them a half share (Hasted's translation, 1800). No rate, toll house or reeve is recorded for 793: the bench, the sticks and the men are invented. The fort wall and its bastions: Kent Archaeological Rescue Unit.

sites.name: The trodden ground before Saint Martin's
sites.see: An open space of beaten chalk and mud between the church door and the fort wall, with thatched houses close round it. Women sell from cloths on the ground: folded lengths of grey and brown wool, cheeses, eels in a wet basket, a few Frankish pots. A man holds two sheep by the horns. Hearth smoke hangs low, a child drives geese through all of it, and the church's wooden gable stands over the whole.
sites.source: No market place is known at Dover in these years (dossier 2 and 8): the ground before the minster is the game's guess, after ports_793.json's kind 'market'. Goods are Kent's at large: wool, cloth and hides out, wine, querns, pots and glass in (Design/research_trade_seasons_and_hints.md).

sites.name: Saint Martin's, the wooden minster
sites.see: A long narrow church of upright oak planks under a shingled roof, grown eastward by one building after another. Inside it is dim and smells of tallow and old wood; the floor is a hard smooth red, like polished stone, and runs up to a stone altar base at the east end. A dozen clerks in dark tunics sing the office from memory. Poor people sit along the outside wall by the south door, waiting for the bread.
sites.source: Rebuilt in wood four times between the 7th and 10th centuries (Kent Archaeological Rescue Unit); lengthened eastward in the late 7th century and floored a century later with 'imitation red marble' (The Dover Historian, 'St Martin-le-Grand', reporting the dig: the floor of 793 if the dating holds (?)); twenty-two canons by the house's tradition (Victoria County History). Believed lost in the fire of 1066 (Dover Museum).

sites.name: The weaving huts under the west wall
sites.see: A row of low huts with their floors dug knee-deep into the chalk, thatch coming down almost to the ground. Through each open door is an upright loom leaning on the wall, its warp threads pulled tight by rings of baked clay as big as a fist. Women beat the weft upward with a bone sword and talk across the lane without looking up. Fleeces soak in a trough; the lane smells of wet wool and stale urine from the dye tub.
sites.source: Sunken-floored buildings inside the fort; one, burnt in the 7th century, held over 200 loom weights (Kent Archaeological Rescue Unit; Dover Museum, 'Saxon Dover'). Weaving here in 793 is carried forward from that find (?).

sites.name: Beornflæd's ale-house
sites.see: A longer house than its neighbours, built against the inside of the fort wall so that one end of the room is Roman flint. A hearth burns down the middle with benches either side; a green bush hangs on a pole over the door when the ale is fresh. Men off the boats sit with their backs to the old wall, pilgrims with their bundles between their feet. It is warm, loud with three kinds of English and one of Frisian, and smells of malt, smoke and drying cloaks.
sites.source: Invented: an ale-house is the news place every port needs. The host answers for a guest kept three nights: laws of Hlothhere and Eadric of Kent, c. 15 (673-686) (?). The ale-bush as a sign is later custom carried back (?). The old steersman's telling: unlocks_793.json text.seafarer.

sites.name: The boat ground up the Dour
sites.see: A bend of the stream a bowshot above the shingle, where the tide still comes. On the bank a small boat stands half planked on blocks, her strakes held with wooden clamps; oak chips lie thick underfoot and a pot of tar smokes over a slow fire. A second boat lies on her side with her bottom being scraped. A man with an adze works and a boy holds the dolly behind each nail. Watercress grows in the shallows.
sites.source: No ship or yard has been found at Dover. Clench nails from boats lay in graves here (unlocks_793.json unlock_ship_west_small_boat, from ship_classes_793.json), and the Dour was tidal well inland (The Dover Historian, 'Dour River', no source given (?)). The yard and the wright are invented.

sites.name: The old light on the east height
sites.see: A steep walk up through thorn and sheep to a grassy bank on the cliff top. Inside the bank stands a tower of eight sides, grey-green stone banded with red tile, as tall as six houses and open to the sky; jackdaws go in and out of its windows. From its foot the whole strait lies open: the shingle and roofs far below, a second broken tower on the western hill, and across the water the cliffs of the Franks. The wind never stops.
sites.source: The eastern Roman lighthouse: eight-sided, of tufa, ragstone and red brick, four Roman stages, about 24 m (Wikipedia en 'Dover Castle', 'St Mary in Castro, Dover'). The western one's state in 793 is unknown. Earthworks on the hill hint at an older fort, unproven. No source says either was lit after the Romans, and the game keeps Dover dark (Design/lighting_and_atmosphere.md). Aldhelm's riddle of the lighthouse: riddles_793.json riddle_aldhelm_92_farus.

sites.name: The old people's graves on Long Hill
sites.see: A long chalk hill east of the stream, grazed short, with rows of low grassy humps running across the slope, some no higher than a furrow. Nobody is buried here now; the dead go to Saint Martin's. Sheep lie on the mounds out of the wind. Where a bank has slipped, a rim of green bronze and a row of rust-red nail heads show in the white chalk. Larks, and the sea far down.
sites.source: The Buckland grave field: 170 graves found in 1951 and 244 more in 1994, with weapons, jewellery, combs, pots and Frankish goods (Dover Museum; Wikipedia en 'Buckland Anglo-Saxon cemetery'); older than the game, about 475-750 (?). Boat nails in Dover graves: ship_classes_793.json. That the mounds still showed in 793 is assumed (?).

sites.name: The moneyer's house
sites.see: A house like the others but for the door, which is oak and barred, and the sound from inside: a hammer on iron, one blow at a time, never two together. Through the hatch a man sits astride a block with a die set in it; a boy lays a blank of silver on, the man sets the upper die and strikes. New pennies lie in a wooden bowl, each with the king's head and, round the back, the moneyer's name and the town's.
sites.source: A mint at Dover by the middle of the 10th century (Dover Museum, 'Saxon Dover'); its house has not been found. English pennies name the moneyer and the mint from Æthelstan's time. No moneyer is named here because none has been checked against the coin record (dossier 3 and 8).

sites.name: Saint Mary's on the height, and the bell tower
sites.see: On the cliff top a new church of knapped flint with corners and arches of red Roman tile, cross-shaped, a square tower over the middle. Close against its west end stands the old eight-sided light tower, with a fresh stage of flint on top and bells in it where the fire used to be. Graves lie all round with plain wooden markers. When the bells ring the sound goes out over the water, and boatmen say they have steered by it in fog.
sites.source: Built about 1000 of flint and Roman tile, cross-shaped with a central tower; the lighthouse made its bell tower with a fifth stage; a large late Saxon graveyard round it (Wikipedia en 'St Mary in Castro, Dover'; Dover Museum). Steering by the bells is the game's (?).

sites.name: The burgesses' hall
sites.see: A big timber hall near the market ground with a carved door-post and a bench along the outside wall, where the men of the town sit in judgement on each other and drink afterwards. Inside is one long room, a raised hearth, shields and oars on the wall and a chest with three locks. The king's reeve has a seat here and so has the earl's man, and the steersmen of the twenty ships sit nearest the fire.
sites.source: Domesday Book names the burgesses' guildhall at Dover (Hasted's translation, 1800); it is on record in 1086 and assumed to stand in King Edward's time (?). The twenty ships, twenty-one men in each, for fifteen days a year, and the king's two parts and the earl's third of the town's dues: the same.

people.name: Wulfric
people.trait: Has crossed the strait more times than he has been to church, and judges every stranger by how they sit in a boat.
people.want: A second boat and a son-in-law to steer her, so the crossing stays in the family.
people.fear: The south-west wind on the ebb, and a new reeve who decides the crossing is the king's to let.
people.voice: Slow and flat, eyes on the water while he talks; counts in tides, not days.
people.looks: About forty, short and thick in the shoulder, a face like tanned hide, a hooded grey cloak stiff with salt, bare feet on the shingle and a bailing scoop hung from his belt.
knows: when the wind will let a boat over, and when it will not let her back
who is waiting on the shingle and what they say they are
what the toll men on the Frankish bank are opening this month
the set of the stream in the strait at each state of the moon
where his sister lodges people at Quentovic and what she charges

ties.note: his sister, a wine man's widow at Quentovic: he sends his passengers to her door and she sends hers to his boat
his dead wife's sister; she feeds his children and tells him so
the reeve wants a penny on every head that crosses
two men who read water: they trade marks, the Maas mouth for the strait, and neither gives the best one
took the Mercian's wife and boy over to see him while his ship lay sealed
the Wantsum men say the long way round by Thanet is the safe one
her cloth crosses under his thwarts, and he has never once asked what she gets for it on the other side
old Lulla taught him the strait and still says he takes the stream too early; Wulfric lets him say it

lines.greet: A Frisian keel. You will ask about the stream. She runs toward the Franks till the moon is south, then she runs back. Do not argue with her.
lines.greet_again: You again. She sat well on the stones last time. Whoever taught you to beach a boat was not a fool.
rumour: Nine on the shingle say they go to the Apostles. Seven walk like pilgrims. Two walk like men who have carried cloth all their lives.
My sister says the toll men over there open every bundle now. She also says the abbot has not said no. With her that is good news.
A boat from Sarre went over on the ebb with the wind behind her. They found the oars at Folkestone.
lines.saying: You can see the other shore from here. That is what drowns people.
lines.to_heir: Your father beached here and paid for the rollers without being asked. Sit down. I knew him before you did.
lines.farewell: Go on the first of the flood, not before. If you see my sister, tell her the boy has her nose and my temper.

people.source: Invented, to answer quentovic.wulfgifu's tie ('her brother keeps a boat on the strand at Dofras'). The office is Domesday's steersman and helper found by the burgesses for the king's messenger (Hasted's translation, 1800), carried back to 793 (?). The stream's turn is modern tide knowledge carried back (Research/water_levels/north_sea_core.md).

people.name: Hereberht
people.trait: A Kentish thegn who took a Mercian king's office and has been explaining it to his neighbours ever since.
people.want: To be on the winning side one more time, and to be seen to have been on it from the start.
people.fear: The day Offa dies, and the men of Kent remember who took his toll for him.
people.voice: Reasonable, a little too loud; says 'the king' quickly and looks to see who heard.
people.looks: Forty-five, tall and going soft, fair hair cut at the jaw, a good blue cloak with a gilt disc brooch, a sword he has never drawn in anger and a horn on a baldric.
knows: what the king has ordered about Frankish hulls, and how far Dofras is from the king
who witnessed which sale, and whose word stands in the folk-moot
which of the pilgrims on the shingle he has decided not to look at
what the men of Kent say about Mercia when they think he is not listening

ties.note: Offa's wic-reeve at Lundenwic: Hereberht copies whatever Wighelm does about Frankish ships, a month late
both are Offa's men in Kent, and the archbishop is the only one who says so kindly
the other half of the toll sits at the other end of his bench
wants the crossing taxed by the head
his blue cloak is hers and half paid for
the reeve at the Stour landing sends him word of what the archbishop's household is buying
she names her guests to him on the third night, as the law says; he would like it to be the first

lines.greet: You are in the king's peace here, and the king's toll. A Frisian is no Frank, so I have no order against you. Stand there while it is counted.
lines.greet_again: The Dorestad man. Good. You pay without making me fetch witnesses. I wish I could say it of my own people.
rumour: The king of the Franks has shut his shore to our merchants, and ours is shut to his. Pilgrims may pass. I have never seen so many pilgrims.
They say the king is sick. They said it last year. I do not listen, and I do not let it be said at my bench.
There is a man called Eadberht who was a priest and says he is of the old Kentish kin. Remember the name. I wish I could forget it.
lines.saying: A reeve is a gate. Nobody thanks a gate.
lines.to_heir: Your father dealt with me when it was not popular to. I remember who did that. There were not many.
lines.farewell: Go with the king's leave. If they ask on the other side who let you sail, say the wind did.

people.source: Invented: no reeve of Dover is named before 1066 (dossier 1 and 3). The king's wic-reeve witnessing sales: laws of Hlothhere and Eadric c. 16 (?). Offa ruled Kent until 29 July 796; Eadberht Praen, by later account a priest, held it 796-798 (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle). He leaves the game with Cenwulf's ravaging in 798: what became of him is the ending of the story dofras.archbishops_chest.

people.name: Cynehelm
people.trait: The canon who keeps Saint Martin's half of the toll and its three books, and is prouder of the tally than he thinks a priest should be.
people.want: A fourth book for the church, a gospel with the pictures in; and the roof made good before he dies.
people.fear: Fire. The church is wood, the town is wood, and he has seen what one spark does to thatch.
people.voice: Dry, exact, fond of a text; ends a bargain with 'Saint Martin thanks you', which means it is closed.
people.looks: Nearly fifty, thin, a clipped grey tonsure, a dark wool tunic to the shin with a plain belt, ink on two fingers and a bundle of notched hazel sticks under his arm.
knows: what the toll took last year and from whom, to the penny
King Wihtred's law, by heart, and which parts of it people still break
which letters have gone over the water and who carried them
what a book costs in calfskins and in years
the feasts and fasts, and which days the boats may not put out

ties.note: the archbishop has no rule over the canons, who answer to Rome and the king; Cynehelm likes him better for it
counts the reeve's half as well as his own, aloud
the guest master of Saint Josse over the water: they send each other the people neither can feed
has tried for thirty years to teach the old man the Creed in the right order
Alcuin's letter-carrier sleeps in the church porch when he waits on the wind, and leaves news instead of alms
the Christ Church scribes lent him a psalter to copy and want it back

lines.greet: Half of what you pay the reeve you pay to Saint Martin. He divided his cloak with a beggar. We divide the toll with a king. Sit.
lines.greet_again: I have your stick here from last time. Paid in full, a clean notch. You would be surprised how few of these I hang up.
rumour: A letter went over at Whitsun with a seal I knew and came back with one I did not. Kings are talking again. Buy wool.
There is a line at our south door every morning. The harvest failed here too. If you have barley, I will find you an honest buyer and a blessing.
King Wihtred's law says a stranger off the track must shout or blow his horn, or be taken for a thief. Half our pilgrims could be hanged on it.
lines.saying: Wood burns, wax melts, kings die. A tally stick, kept dry, outlasts all three.
lines.to_heir: Your father's name is in our book, among those we pray for at Martinmas. He paid for that, and for a good deal of bread.
lines.farewell: Saint Martin thanks you. Go carefully. The sea is no respecter of receipts.

people.source: Invented: no canon of Saint Martin's is named before Domesday (dossier 3). The canons as secular clerks 'subject to no one except the court of Rome and the king', their half of the toll and their common fund: Victoria County History, Kent, vol. 2. Wihtred's law on the stranger: Wikipedia (en) 'Law of Wihtred' (our wording). Saint Martin's cloak: Sulpicius Severus, Vita Martini 3.

people.name: Hildgyth
people.trait: The best weaver under the west wall, with six looms and four daughters, and a memory for every cloak she ever sold and to whom.
people.want: To sell over the water herself and not through men who call themselves pilgrims and take the half.
people.fear: That the Franks really will want every cloak a different length, and she will be left with a winter's work nobody buys.
people.voice: Quick, plain, never stops working while she talks; asks what things cost before she asks your name.
people.looks: Thirty-five, strong forearms, brown hair under a linen head-cloth, a russet gown pinned with two small bronze brooches, a bone weaving-sword in her hand and wool fluff on everything.
knows: the price of wool this midsummer and what it will be at Michaelmas
what length and what colour the Frankish buyers ask for now
whose bundle on the shingle is full of her cloaks
which dye holds in sea water and which runs

ties.note: Wulfgifu sells her cloaks from the house at Quentovic and sends back the price, less a fair share, by her brother's boat
he owes her: half the price of a blue cloak, two winters old
they were girls together and share one opinion of the reeve
her goods cross in his boat under the thwarts
the Dorestad skipper buys English cloth by the shipload at Hamwic and sells it over there as Frisian
a cousin among the cloak-makers of the Strand, who asks her in every message why the Franks want them longer
Thiadbod's man on the West Saxon beach, whose knots she finds on bundles of cloth that should have crossed in her own name

lines.greet: Feel that. Go on, with your thumb. That is two fleeces and eleven days. Now, what do they give for it at Dorestad? Do not lie.
lines.greet_again: You came back, so you sold them. What did the Frisians say about the length? Too short, I suppose. Everyone is a king now.
rumour: The king of the Franks says our cloaks are too short to cover him in bed or keep the rain off him on a horse. Let him ride less.
One of those pilgrims on the stones has thirty of my cloaks in his bundle and a psalm on his lips. He prays well. I taught him the price.
Wool is dear already and it is not yet Lammas. Somebody is buying for the Mercian king's men. Buy now or do not buy.
lines.saying: A long cloak for a long purse. I cut to the purse.
lines.to_heir: Your father carried my cloth and brought back the true price. Most bring back a story. Are you his son or only his heir?
lines.farewell: Keep it dry and keep it folded with the nap in. And if they say it is short, say it is Kentish.

people.source: Invented. Weaving at Dover: over 200 loom weights in one burnt building of the 7th century (Kent Archaeological Rescue Unit). The king's complaint of short cloaks is Notker's story of Charles and the Frisian cloaks (Gesta Karoli I.34, about 885; our wording, after the sense of Grant 1907), and Charles's letter to Offa of 796 asks that cloaks be of the old length (MGH Epistolae IV no. 100).

people.name: Beornflæd
people.trait: Keeps the house under the wall where everyone waits for the wind, answers to the reeve for each of them, and forgets nothing said after the third cup.
people.want: Her sister's children fed and her nephew kept off the boats until he can swim, which he will not learn.
people.fear: A guest who does harm on his third night under her roof, for which the law makes her pay.
people.voice: Warm and unhurried, with a question tucked inside every kindness.
people.looks: About forty, broad and upright, a clean linen head-cloth, a green gown with the sleeves pushed up, keys and a small knife on a girdle, a wooden ladle never far from her hand.
knows: who is lodged in the town tonight, where from, and what they said they were
which crewmen are loose and looking for a berth
what the last boat over brought back as news, and how old it was
who owes whom in Dofras

ties.note: her dead sister's husband: she raises his children and keeps his accounts honest
friends from girlhood
the old man has the seat by the hearth for nothing, because people come to hear him
names her guests to him on the third night, as the law says, and not a night sooner
sisters by marriage: one house on each shore, and a traveller handed from one to the other
the house at the Wantsum ferry says its ale is stronger; it is only newer
the ale-wife on the Strand says pilgrims will say anything; Beornflæd says that is why she listens to them
her house by the wall stays in the family: a steersman of King Edward's day says his people have brewed there since the old kings (?)

lines.greet: Sit by the old wall, it holds the heat. Two nights you are a guest. The third night I answer for you, so tell me now what you are.
lines.greet_again: There you are. Your bench is free and so is the first cup. Now, what are they saying at Dorestad? I have people waiting to hear.
rumour: The Northumbrian in the corner has not spoken for two days. Somebody told him what was done on the holy island. He had a brother there.
Two men of mine want a berth. One is good and drinks. One is sober and cannot steer. Take your pick, I will not tell you which is which.
The clerk says the reeve's half of the toll came out lighter than Saint Martin's last month. Same ships. Think about that.
lines.saying: Ale tells you what a man is. The wind decides how long I have to listen.
lines.to_heir: You have his way of looking at the door before you sit. He lodged here every crossing for twenty years and left owing nothing.
lines.farewell: God keep you over the water. Come back by this door and tell me what was true.

people.source: Invented. The host's answering for a guest of three nights: laws of Hlothhere and Eadric of Kent c. 15 (673-686) (?). The guest who looks at every door: Hávamál 1 (Bellows 1923) (a Norse saying, used here only as a habit seen). News of Lindisfarne, 8 June 793: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 793.

people.name: Lulla
people.trait: An old steersman who can no longer pull an oar, so he climbs to the dead light every fair morning to count sails, and comes down every evening to say what he saw.
people.want: Someone to learn the long song from him before it goes into the ground with him.
people.fear: A morning when he cannot make the climb.
people.voice: Half speaks, half chants; drops into verse without noticing and out of it without finishing.
people.looks: Close on seventy, stooped and long-armed, white hair to the shoulder, pale eyes that water in the wind, a patched sheepskin over a grey tunic and a tall thorn staff worn smooth at the grip.
knows: every sail in the strait this week, by her cut and her course
the signs of weather from the height: the far shore too clear, gulls inland, a swell with no wind in it
The Seafarer, entire, and a great many riddles
what the old people said the towers were for

ties.note: taught Wulfric the strait, and still tells him he takes the stream too early
pays for his seat in songs
argues with the clerk about whether the giants or the Romans built the towers
the Frisian pilot brings him a cheese each time and asks the same question about the Goodwin sands
knows a lookout when he sees one: he and your Northumbrian can sit an hour on the height and say nothing
the Hamwic pilot, who passes word of sails along the coast and has the same song with a different ending, and is wrong
a ploughman on the down at Sarre counts the same sails from the other side of the Foreland; a boy runs between them with the number (?)

lines.greet: I saw you come in from the top. You held too far east and the stream carried you right. That is luck or knowledge. Which?
lines.greet_again: The Frisian with the brown sail. I knew you at the Foreland. Sit. I will tell you what else is out there.
rumour: Three sails went west under the far shore at first light, close together, low in the water. Not fishermen. I did not like their keeping together.
The far cliffs stood up sharp as a knife this morning. When you can count the Franks' sheep, do not sail. Rain by dark, wind after.
The clerk says Romans built the towers. My grandfather said giants. Either way nobody alive could, so what is the difference?
lines.saying: A tower with no fire is still a mark. An old man with no oar is still a steersman.
lines.to_heir: I taught your father one song and he taught me a Frisian word for fog. I have forgotten the word. He kept the song, I hope.
lines.farewell: I will watch you out. If I lift the staff, come back. If I do not, I have fallen asleep, and go on.

people.source: Invented, to carry unlocks_793.json text.seafarer ('told by an old English steersman who has it by heart, for an evening's ale', at Dofras). Weather signs: Design/npc_text_encounters.md 1.2. 'The work of giants' for Roman stone is the Old English poets' phrase (The Ruin; Maxims II), used here as a belief, not quoted. The Goodwin sands by that name are later (?).

people.name: Godwine
people.trait: Earl of the West Saxons and of Kent, the greatest man in England under the king, who has the third penny of this town and knows its steersmen by name.
people.want: His house kept great and his sons in their earldoms; the king's French friends sent home.
people.fear: That the king will remember, when it suits him, how the king's brother Alfred died.
people.voice: Easy and warm with shipmen, quite still when he is angry; never raises his voice and never needs to.
people.looks: About fifty, big and broad, grey in a full moustache, a red cloak with a gold ring-brooch on the shoulder, a sword with a silvered hilt, and housecarls in mail a few paces behind him.
knows: how many ships each harbour between here and Wight owes, and who steers them
what the king has ordered, and whose counsel it was
who in Flanders will lend ships to an English earl
what was done at Dofras when the Frenchmen came, house by house

ties.note: Cnut made him an earl and gave him a Danish wife; all he has began there
one of the town's steersmen: the earl would not burn his house, and Godric has not forgotten
Count Baldwin of Flanders shelters him over the winter of his exile, at Bruges (?)
the port-reeve at Canterbury's landing gathers the earl's third penny of Fordwic, and is careful that it is a full third
the king's port-reeve in London has the writ; the earl has the shipmen

lines.greet: A merchant of the Rhine mouth. Your people have beached here longer than mine have held it. Sit. Tell me what is said in Flanders.
lines.greet_again: I know you. You were on the strand when it mattered. I do not forget a face from a bad day.
rumour: The king told me to carry fire into Dofras for defending its own doors. I told him these are my people. That is all that passed between us.
The Frenchmen put on their mail before they came into the town. A guest does not arm himself to ask for a bed.
I have asked each harbour for ships and for men's sons as pledges. I take no more than I am given. I am given a great deal.
lines.saying: A king can outlaw an earl. He cannot outlaw a coast.
lines.to_heir: Your house carried a word for mine once, over the water, when few would. My sons know it. That is worth more than my thanks.
lines.farewell: Sail when you like. No ship of mine will stop you, and this year that is most of the ships there are.

people.source: Godwine, earl of Wessex from about 1020, died 15 April 1053 (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle); his birth year is a guess (?). His third part of Dover's dues: Domesday Book (Hasted's translation, 1800). 1051: he would not go against Dover, being 'loth to injure his own people' (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle E, Avalon Project); 1052: he and Harold took ships and hostages here. He can be met in 1042-1051 on his rounds and in the summer of 1052; he is in exile from the autumn of 1051. The role 'count' stands for an earl: there is no earl in npc_roles_793.json. The words given him are ours, not the Chronicle's.

people.name: Godric
people.trait: A burgess with a house by the market ground and the steering oar of one of the town's twenty ships, who carries the king's messengers over and thinks the town has paid for its freedoms twice.
people.want: His sons quit of toll after him, and one year with no summons for the ships.
people.fear: Mailed men at his door again. He has seen it once.
people.voice: Blunt, a little weary; tells a bad story the same way every time, like evidence.
people.looks: Forty, square and weathered, cropped brown hair and a moustache, a knee-length green tunic with a plain belt and a long knife, a steersman's horn slung at his back, a scar through one eyebrow.
knows: the passage money: three pennies a horse in winter, two in summer, and who must find the extra hands
what the town owes the king in ships and days, and what it gets for them
what happened in each house when Count Eustace's men came
which Wissant men can be trusted with a rope

ties.note: gave the earl a ship in 1052 and a nephew as pledge, both freely
by the family telling, the house by the wall where his people have brewed since the old kings (?)
as a boy at the oar he lay at Sandwich with the king's ships, where old Leofnoth of the Wantsum counted the Dofras hulls and the Sandwich hulls alike (?)
learned the steering oar as a boy in a ship called out for King Cnut
his father paid into the three thousand pounds of 1009 and told him the sum every winter until he died
the port-reeve at Fordwic tolls the burgesses of Dofras though they go quit through all England, and gives it back slowly

lines.greet: You will pay toll, because you do not live here. I do, and I pay the king in ships, and go quit through all England. Think on it.
lines.greet_again: The Frisian house. Come in. You were told the passage price fairly last time, and you will be again. Three in winter, two in summer.
rumour: They armed themselves on the hill before they came in. One wanted my neighbour's house. He wounded my neighbour. My neighbour killed him. Then they all came.
More than twenty of ours dead, in and out of doors. Nineteen of theirs. Then the king sends to have us harried for it. The earl said no.
From Michaelmas to Saint Andrew the king's peace lies on this town. Break it then and the reeve takes the fine from everyone alike.
lines.saying: We owe the king fifteen days a year. He remembers the days. We remember the year.
lines.to_heir: Your father stood in the lane with us and did not have to. There is a seat for his son in the hall. It is not offered twice.
lines.farewell: Wind is fair for Wissant. If a Boulogne man asks where you lay last night, say Sandwich.

people.source: Invented: the wounded householder of 1051 and his neighbours are unnamed (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle E 1048 for 1051, Avalon Project: more than twenty townsmen and nineteen of the count's men killed). The ship service, the passage of the king's messengers at 3 d and 2 d a horse, the steersman and his helper, quittance of toll through all England for a resident burgess who paid the king's custom, and the king's peace from Michaelmas to Saint Andrew: Domesday Book in Hasted's translation (1800), of King Edward's time. Wissant as the crossing is on record only from about this time (Wikipedia en 'Wissant'). The 3,000 pounds of 1009: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle.

stories.title: Nine for the Apostles
stories.summary: While King Charles's shore is shut to English merchants, pilgrims may still cross, and nine people wait on the shingle for a boat to Quentovic. Seven are what they say; two have thirty Kentish cloaks in a bundle and a share to offer whoever carries them past the Frankish toll.
stories.picture: Grey morning on a shingle bank: a knot of cloaked pilgrims with staffs sitting on their bundles beside a beached Frisian boat, one man's bundle twice the size of the rest, a white cliff behind.

beats.text: Pilgrims ask a passage to Quentovic: no silver, they say, only prayers and their hands at the oars. Wulfric says two of them walk like men who have carried cloth all their lives.
Hildgyth knows the bundle: thirty of her cloaks, cut to the length she has always cut. She would sooner you carried them openly and brought her the true price than see a false pilgrim take the half.
Hereberht has decided not to look at pilgrims' bundles. He will look if you ask him to, and remember that you asked.
Every pilgrim on the shingle carries a letter of passage in a Christ Church hand. The scribe who wrote them asks skippers what a man bound for the Apostles wants with twelve cloaks.
Three more wait at the Sarre crossing with one bundle between them. The ferryman carried it and says it was heavier than their sins. If that cloth is Hildgyth's too, nobody has told her.
On the West Saxon beach a Frisian ropes cloaks into square bundles for six more pilgrims. Hildgyth has seen his knots on the Canche side, and calls him the man who taught poverty to carry.
On the Frankish bank the abbot's clerk counts heads and looks at hands. A Frisian keel with English pilgrims is lawful. English cloaks in her are not.
After the king's letter true pilgrims pass free and traders pay in the proper place. The clerk opens every bundle on the bank and asks you which of your passengers is which.
Wulfgifu, Wulfric's sister, sells the cloaks from her house whichever way they came, and sends the price back by whoever she trusts. After this she knows whether that is you.

Hildgyth's cousin among the cloak-makers of the Strand asks the question all of them ask: why do the Franks want them longer? Whoever brings a measured answer sells the first cloaks of the new length.

endings.how: You carried the pilgrims free and declared the cloaks at the Frankish toll as Hildgyth's goods in a Frisian hull.
endings.text: The tenth is paid and the cloaks are sold in daylight. The false pilgrim loses his half and Hildgyth gains it. She weaves to your order after that, and to the Frankish length when you bring it.
endings.reward: Hildgyth a fast friend; the unlock dofras.unlock.hildgyths_looms; the deeds fair_dealing and gave_alms; flag dofras_bundle_declared.

endings.how: You said nothing, carried the bundle as a pilgrim's, and took a share of the sale.
endings.text: Thirty cloaks pass as one man's bedding. The share is good silver. The clerk at Quentovic looks at you a moment longer next time, and the man with the bundle now knows a Frisian who will.
endings.reward: Silver at once (a third of the cloaks' price, about 60 d (?)); the false pilgrim as a man who remembers you; a risk at the Quentovic toll on later calls; flag dofras_bundle_hidden.

endings.how: You told the reeve at Dofras whose bundle it was.
endings.text: Hereberht takes the cloaks for the king and one for himself. He is your friend while he lasts, which is until 798. Hildgyth is paid nothing and knows who spoke.
endings.reward: Hereberht friendly and the toll lightened while he holds office; Hildgyth and Beornflæd cool for years; flag dofras_bundle_told.

endings.how: You would not carry them at all.
endings.text: They wait for another boat. Wulfric shrugs. It costs nothing but the seven honest ones' prayers.
endings.reward: Nothing gained and nothing lost; the story can be taken up again on a later call while the shore is shut.

stories.reward: A weaver on one shore and a seller on the other who know you by name: Kentish cloaks at the loom's price, and an honest price sent home.

stories.title: The chest under the red floor
stories.summary: In the summer of 796 Offa dies, Kent rises under Eadberht Praen, and the archbishop, Offa's man, leaves Canterbury. In the game a clerk of his household reaches Dofras at night with a chest of the church's books and no boat, and three people want that chest for three different reasons.
stories.picture: Night inside a wooden church: a clerk and a thin priest lifting a board of a red floor by one candle, an iron-bound chest beside them, a Frisian skipper holding the door.

beats.text: The archbishop's people crossed the Wantsum at night with a chest and no torches, and the ferryman was paid in a blessing. He will say which road the mule took, for a cup; which road the archbishop took he does not know.

A clerk of Christ Church has come over the downs with a mule and a chest: a gospel book, a psalter and the church's charters. The archbishop has gone another way. Cynehelm will hide the chest, but wood burns, and he wants it over the water.
Hereberht's bench is empty one morning and a man of Eadberht's sits there. He is looking for anything that belonged to the Mercian's archbishop, and he pays for news.
Wulfric will not take the chest: his boat is known. A Frisian keel is nobody's business. He will show you the hour of the tide and say nothing after.
At the cell of Saint Josse the guest master Osmund takes the chest in, writes a receipt on a scrap, and reads you a line from his abbot Alcuin, who has told the archbishop to go back to his flock.
At Saint Paul's the priest Eanwulf has the archbishop's letters and nobody honest to carry them. He asks whether the books got out of Kent, and writes the answer in a hand small enough to hide.
The archbishop is home, and Kent is quiet because it is ruined. He asks who carried the books. If the answer is you, he has a seat for you and a letter to anyone you name.

endings.how: You carried the chest to Saint Josse and brought the receipt back.
endings.text: The books winter with Alcuin's monks and come home in 798 in the same hull. Cynehelm writes your name in Saint Martin's book. The archbishop does not forget a Frisian who asked no fee.
endings.reward: Æthelheard and Cynehelm fast friends; the unlock dofras.unlock.saint_martins_half; a copy of one text from the chest for your own (act:copy_text free at the minster); the deed carried_letters; flag dofras_chest_carried.

endings.how: You helped Cynehelm bury the chest under the church floor and kept quiet when you were asked.
endings.text: It lies under the red floor for two years. Eadberht's man finds nothing. When the Mercians come in 798 they find nothing either, and Cynehelm digs it up himself.
endings.reward: Cynehelm a fast friend; free lodging in the minster's guest house for the house; flag dofras_chest_hidden. Nothing from the archbishop: he never learns your name.

endings.how: You told Eadberht's man where the chest was.
endings.text: The charters go to the new king, who has uses for them; the gospel book's cover is worth its weight. You are paid well, and Kent is yours for two years. Then Cenwulf comes.
endings.reward: Silver at once (about 120 d (?)); standing with the Kentish until 798 and a welcome from Eadberht's reeve; after 798 the archbishop's door at Fordwic is shut to the house for a generation; flag dofras_chest_sold.

stories.reward: The friendship of the minster, or of an archbishop, or two years of a doomed king's favour: and a text from the chest, if the chest was kept safe.

stories.title: The tower with no fire
stories.summary: Old Lulla climbs every morning to a tower that once showed ships their road and now holds jackdaws. He has a riddle about it he cannot read and a song he wants to leave to someone; in 811 a fire is lit on the far shore, and a merchant can decide whether this shore answers.
stories.picture: An old man with a staff at the foot of an eight-sided ruined tower on a cliff top at dusk, looking across dark water at one small point of fire on the far shore.

beats.text: Lulla counts sails from the foot of the old light and says what the weather will do. Sit with him three mornings and he begins the long song, a piece at a time.
For an evening's ale he tells The Seafarer entire, and Beornflæd's house goes quiet for it. Afterwards he asks you a riddle of his own about a thing that stands on a cliff and has lost its eye.
Cynehelm knows there is a Latin riddle of Bishop Aldhelm's about a very high lighthouse on the rocks of the sea. He has heard it, and does not own it. A school on the Rhine does.
Abbot Lull at Dommoc has Aldhelm's lighthouse by heart and sets it to visiting masters. One who has stood at the foot of the tower at Dofras answers before the abbot has finished, which annoys him.

At the mouth of the Orwell an old stone fort stands on its cliff with round towers at the corners. The fowler says giants built it, and that he has never seen a fire on it either. The sea takes a piece each winter.
The pilot at Hamwic has the long song too, with a different ending. Lulla says the West Saxon is wrong. Whoever has heard both may say so to either of them, at his own risk.
On a clear night a fire shows on the far shore: the emperor has lit the tower at Boulogne. The watcher on the height asks why the Franks have a light and the English have a ruin.
A cleric of the archbishop sells Aldhelm's riddle of the lighthouse. A merchant of your house who has stood at the foot of the tower at Dofras knows the answer before the reading is done.
The tower has bells in it now. The ringer says his people have always watched from here, and that some Frisian once paid for a fire. Whether he is right depends on what your house did.

endings.how: You sat with Lulla until he had told the whole song, and had it written or learned by one of your crew.
endings.text: He dies in 808 with the song handed on. Your lookout tells it on night watches for the rest of his life, and the crew's heart is better for it.
endings.reward: The text seafarer in the chest (unlocks_793.json text.seafarer); Lulla's weather signs for the strait (the day stick shows the next day's wind at Dofras); flag dofras_song_kept.

endings.how: You paid for the watch fire on the east height (the work dofras.work.beacon).
endings.text: A basket of fire burns beside the old tower on nights when boats are out. It is not the Romans' light, but boatmen find the gap in the cliffs by it, and they know whose fire it is.
endings.reward: The work's gains; the watchers of the height serve the house for good (a warning of any fleet in the strait before you sail); when the lighthouse riddle is met it is answered as 'sure'; flag dofras_fire_lit.

endings.how: You heard the old man out once and went on your way.
endings.text: The tower stays a mark by day and nothing by night, as it was. The song goes into the ground with Lulla, or to someone else's lookout.
endings.reward: One evening's telling, which lifts the crew's heart that night and no longer.

stories.reward: A song for the chest, a watcher who warns you of fleets in the strait, and the answer to a riddle another port sells.

stories.title: Their own doors
stories.summary: In 1009 the town pays its part of three thousand pounds to Thorkell's army; in 1051 it fights a count's mailed men in its own lanes and the king orders it burnt for that; in 1052 the earl who would not burn it comes back for its ships. In October 1066 nobody refuses the order.
stories.picture: A narrow lane between thatched houses: townsmen with axes and boat hooks in their doorways facing mailed riders, a woman dragging a child indoors, smoke starting at the lane's end.

beats.text: Thorkell's army lies at Sandwich and east Kent buys peace for three thousand pounds. The town's part is being gathered on a cloth before the church, and a stranger with silver is asked, politely, what Dofras is worth to him.

Godric explains the bargain: twenty ships for fifteen days, the king's messengers carried over, and for that a burgess who lives here goes quit of toll through all England. A man with a plot and a hearth in the town could be such a burgess.

The burgesses of Dofras go quit of toll through all England. At Canterbury's landing the port-reeve Bruman tolls them all the same, and gives it back slowly when a steersman comes with the hall behind him.

Count Eustace's men have armed themselves on the hill and come in demanding beds. One wounds a householder and is killed for it. Then it is every lane at once. You are in the town, with a crew, and a boat on the shingle.
The king has heard the count's side only and has ordered Earl Godwine to carry war into Kent and to Dofras. The earl will not. By Michaelmas he is outlawed and gone over the sea to Baldwin's land.
The earl winters in Flanders gathering ships. A merchant who knows Dofras can tell him which steersmen will come out for him, or tell the king's men at Sandwich what he is gathering.
Godwine and Harold come along the coast and take as many ships and hostages as they choose. Godric gives a ship and a nephew. The earl asks what your house gives.

From Dofras the earl's ships go round by Sandwich and through the Wantsum to the North-mouth. The island that denied twenty-five raiders landing and water four years before stands on the bank and watches Englishmen go by.

The duke has come from Hastings. The town is yielding when his men fire the stronghold on the height, and the wind takes it down into the thatch. There is one tide to load what can be carried, and more people on the shingle than a keel can hold.

endings.how: In 1051 you stood with the townsmen, and in 1052 gave the earl a ship or a man.
endings.text: Your house has a seat in the burgesses' hall and its name with the earl's sons. For fourteen years it trades as a Dofras house. In 1066 that is the wrong name to have.
endings.reward: Godric and Godwine fast friends; the unlock dofras.unlock.quit_of_toll without waiting the year; a place in the town's ships (unlocks_793.json unlock_ship_warship_west); under the Norman king the house is marked as Godwine's (standing with the new lords falls); flag dofras_stood_1051.

endings.how: In 1051 you gave the Frenchmen lodging or carried the count's wounded away to Boulogne.
endings.text: Count Eustace remembers a Frisian who was civil. The town remembers too. You do not beach at Dofras for a generation, and you have a friend on the far shore who comes back in 1066 on the winning side.
endings.reward: The favour of the count of Boulogne (toll forgiven on the Frankish shore of the strait; a word with the duke's men in 1066); Dofras shut to the house until an heir makes it good; flag dofras_lodged_1051.

endings.how: In October 1066 you threw out cargo to take people off the shingle.
endings.text: The keel goes off deep with women, children and one chest from Saint Martin's. The cargo burns on the beach with the town. Those who were carried tell it in every harbour from Sandwich to Wight.
endings.reward: The cargo is lost; the deed gave_alms many times over and standing in every English port; the canons' chest gives one text; the house's name is in the last entry of its own story; flag dofras_last_tide.

endings.how: You kept to the boat each time and sailed when it was over.
endings.text: Nobody blames a stranger for it. Nobody keeps a seat for him either.
endings.reward: Nothing lost. The news of each year, carried fresh to the next port, sells for what such news is worth.

stories.reward: A burgess's freedom from toll in all England, an earl's friendship, or a count's: and the choice of what the house is called when the Normans come.

works.name: A plot inside the old wall
works.what: A house-plot against the Roman wall near the south gate, fenced with wattle, with leave to build a sunk hut for goods and a hearth-house over it. The ground is the king's and the rent is paid to his reeve.
works.needs: To be known in the town (standing 20), and two householders to speak for you before the reeve.
works.gives: A place of your own at Dofras: room for goods under lock, free lodging, and the first step to being a burgess. From 1042, a year and a day lived on it and the king's custom paid opens dofras.unlock.quit_of_toll. It burns in October 1066.
works.picture: A wattle fence marking a small square of ground against a tall flint-and-tile Roman wall, a half-dug hut pit, two townsmen pointing out the bounds to a merchant.
works.source: works_793.json plot (the shared work and its cost). Anglo-Saxon houses inside the fort walls: Kent Archaeological Rescue Unit. The burgess's quittance: Domesday Book (Hasted's translation, 1800). That a stranger could take a plot in 793 is assumed (?).

works.name: A guest house for those who wait on the wind
works.what: A long timber house by Saint Martin's south door with a hearth, straw and a daily loaf, for pilgrims and the poor who must wait for a boat. The canons keep it; your silver builds it.
works.needs: Alms given at the minster at least once, and Cynehelm or his successor friendly.
works.gives: The deed gave_alms many times over; the house lodges free at Dofras for good; pilgrims and letter-carriers ask for your boat first; the canons take their half of the toll lightly from you.
works.picture: A new thatched timber hall beside a wooden church, smoke through the roof, a row of pilgrims with staffs at its door and a clerk handing out loaves from a basket.
works.source: works_793.json hospice. Guests received as Christ: Rule of Saint Benedict 53 (the canons are clerks, not monks, and keep it by custom). English pilgrims crossing to Francia: Charles to Offa, 796 (MGH Epistolae IV no. 100). No hospice is recorded at Dover before the 12th century: this one is the player's (?).

works.name: A watch fire on the east height
works.what: An iron basket on a post beside the old light tower, a stack of furze and driftwood under a hurdle roof, and a man paid to burn it on nights when boats are known to be out. It is not the Romans' fire: the tower itself stays dark.
works.needs: The watcher on the height willing (Lulla, or whoever keeps the watch after him), and the reeve's leave.
works.gives: Coming in to Dofras by night or in thick weather the grounding check is passed more easily; a warning at the strand when a fleet is seen in the strait; the boatmen of the strand think well of the house.
works.picture: A fire basket blazing on a post at night beside the dark bulk of an eight-sided tower, a man feeding it with furze, far below the faint line of surf.
works.source: works_793.json beacon. Invented for the player: no source says either Dover tower was lit after the Romans, and the game's own rule keeps Dover dark (Design/lighting_and_atmosphere.md). The Franks' answer on the other shore: Annales regni Francorum 811.

works.name: Saint Martin's raised again
works.what: After the fire: new oak posts on the old lines, plank walls, a shingled roof and the red floor relaid, so that the canons sing under cover before the second winter.
works.needs: The minster burnt (the game's year is 860), and the canons' goodwill. Oak must be carted from the Weald side.
works.gives: The house's name in Saint Martin's book for as long as there are canons; the canons' half of the toll forgiven to the house for good; a grave for the house's dead inside the church.
works.picture: A timber church half built on a burnt plot: new pale posts standing among black stumps, carpenters raising a roof truss, clerks singing in the open under a hide awning.
works.source: works_793.json church_rebuilt. The church burnt in the 9th century and rebuilt on the same lines: The Dover Historian, 'St Martin-le-Grand' (2014), reporting the Kent Archaeological Rescue Unit's dig. No cause and no year is recorded; nobody is said to have paid for it (?).

works.name: A bell for the old light tower
works.what: A cast bronze bell, bought over the water or poured in a pit at the tower's foot, hung in the new top stage of the Roman tower beside Saint Mary's.
works.needs: Saint Mary's built on the height (about 1000), and a founder brought from Canterbury or from the Franks.
works.gives: The bell is rung in fog and when a boat is overdue: coming in to Dofras in fog is safer for every ship of the house. The house is prayed for on the hill, and the ringer is the house's man.
works.picture: Men hauling a bronze bell on ropes up the outside of an eight-sided tower banded in red tile, a small flint church beside it, the sea grey below.
works.source: works_793.json bell. The lighthouse made a bell tower with a fifth stage when Saint Mary's was built, about 1000: Wikipedia (en) 'St Mary in Castro, Dover'. Who gave the bells is not recorded (?).

ships.how: bought second-hand from a boatman of the strand, or built by the boat ground up the Dour in six weeks
ships.note: The boat of this beach: six metres, four oars, a small sail, light enough to haul above the weed line on rollers. Every crossing boat here is one of these or her big sister.
ships.picture: A small clinker boat hauled up on a shingle bank on log rollers, oars lashed inboard, white cliff behind.
ships.source: ship_classes_793.json west_small_boat; unlocks_793.json unlock_ship_west_small_boat (150 d, at Dofras among others). Clench nails from such boats in graves at Dover.

ships.how: built to order over a winter at the boat ground up the Dour, or bought from the canons when they replace theirs
ships.note: A beach-landing sailing and rowing boat of eight to twelve metres, the kind a minster keeps for its own errands and a ferryman for the crossing: built to take the ground twice a day.
ships.picture: A broad open boat with a short mast sitting upright on shingle at low water, a clerk and two boatmen loading sacks over her side.
ships.source: ship_classes_793.json coaster_minster_ship. That Saint Martin's kept one is assumed from the canons' share in the port's toll (?).

ships.how: bought second-hand, when a keel is sold on the shingle by a dead man's kin; not built here
ships.note: No yard at Dofras builds a sea-going keel: the timber goes to the minster and the beach is too steep. Now and then one changes hands here, because this is where voyages end early.
ships.picture: A broad merchant keel lying over on her bilge on a shingle beach, a small group of people in mourning cloaks bargaining beside her.
ships.source: ship_classes_793.json north_sea_merchant_ship. No ship is found or recorded at Dover in these years: the second-hand sale is the game's (?).

ships.how: not bought: a place at the steering oar of one of the town's ships, by the burgesses' leave
ships.note: In King Edward's time the burgesses owe the king twenty ships for fifteen days in the year, twenty-one men in each. A man of standing who lives in the town may be given one to steer and to man.
ships.picture: A long low ship with twenty oars run out, a steersman with a horn at the stern, more like her drawn up in a row on the shingle under white cliffs.
ships.source: Domesday Book, Dover (Hasted's translation, 1800); ship_classes_793.json warship_west; unlocks_793.json unlock_ship_warship_west (at Dofras from 800 with standing: the town's own twenty are on record only for King Edward's time).

sayings.text: You can see the other shore from here. That is what drowns people.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner (the boatmen of the strand); the two shores in sight of each other: Wikipedia (en) 'Strait of Dover'

sayings.text: A friend is good, far or near; the nearer, the more use.
sayings.source: Durham Proverbs no. 2 (an 11th-century collection), our rendering (?)

sayings.text: What is the good of these little rags? In bed I cannot cover myself with one, on a horse it keeps off neither wind nor rain. (King Charles, on the short cloaks the Frisians sold him at the old price.)
sayings.source: Notker of Saint Gall, Gesta Karoli I.34 (about 885), retold in our own words after the sense of A. J. Grant's translation (1907); told at Dofras by the weavers, against the king

sayings.text: A stranger off the track should shout or blow his horn. A merchant should do both, and then show his silver.
sayings.source: The first half is the law of Wihtred of Kent, c. 28 (695), and of Ine of Wessex, c. 20, our wording; the second half is invented

sayings.text: He divided his cloak with a beggar. We divide the toll with a king.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner (the canons of Saint Martin); the cloak: Sulpicius Severus, Vita Martini 3; the toll: Victoria County History, Kent, vol. 2

sayings.text: This year came Eustace up at Dofras, and his men would lodge where they liked. The townsmen slew nineteen men on the one side, and lost more than twenty on the other.
sayings.source: After the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle (E) 1048 for 1051 (Ingram 1823 / Giles 1847, Avalon Project), shortened and in our own order of words: a retelling, not a quotation

sayings.text: Giants built it, Romans lit it, jackdaws keep it.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; Roman stonework as 'the work of giants' is the Old English poets' phrase (The Ruin; Maxims II)

sayings.text: A riddle for the bench: I stand on a cliff and showed ships their road. My eye is out, and they steer by me still. Say what I am. (A tower with no fire.)
sayings.source: invented, after Aldhelm's riddle 92, 'Farus editissima' (riddles_793.json riddle_aldhelm_92_farus), which is not quoted

easter_eggs.text: The minster floor is a smooth hard red that looks like polished stone and is not: lime and crushed Roman tile, laid and rubbed. Cynehelm will tell you it is marble from Rome. Ask the wright, who has mended it.
easter_eggs.source: The floor sealed with 'imitation red marble' in the 8th century: The Dover Historian, 'St Martin-le-Grand', reporting the Kent Archaeological Rescue Unit's dig. The recipe is a guess (?).

easter_eggs.text: Where the bank has slipped on Long Hill a row of rust-red nail heads shows in the chalk, each bent over a small square plate: a boat's nails, with no boat left round them. Someone was buried with part of his boat over him.
easter_eggs.source: Clench nails from boats in graves at Dover: ship_classes_793.json west_small_boat. The Buckland grave field: Wikipedia (en) 'Buckland Anglo-Saxon cemetery'.

easter_eggs.text: A man digging a well by the stream says he struck black oak planks deep in the mud, sewn together with twisted yew and no nail in them, and filled the hole in again because it was older than Christians. Nobody believes him.
easter_eggs.source: The Dover Bronze Age boat, of about 1575-1520 BC, sewn with yew, lies six metres under the town and was found in 1992 (Wikipedia en 'Dover Bronze Age Boat'). That anyone touched it in these years is invented.

easter_eggs.text: In one of the weaving huts the floor is black a hand's depth down, and full of baked clay rings: more than two hundred. The hut burnt with every loom standing, in somebody's great-grandmother's day, and they built the new one on top.
easter_eggs.source: A sunken-floored building burnt in the 7th century with over 200 loom weights: Kent Archaeological Rescue Unit; Dover Museum, 'Saxon Dover'.

easter_eggs.text: From the east height on a clear day you can count three things nobody alive could build: this tower, its broken fellow on the western hill, and, as a pale stump across the water, the tower of Boulogne.
easter_eggs.source: The two Roman lighthouses flanking the harbour (Dover Museum, 'Roman Dover'; Wikipedia en 'Dubris'); the tower at Boulogne repaired and lit in 811 (Annales regni Francorum). Whether Boulogne's tower shows from Dover by day is not checked (?).

easter_eggs.text: After 868 a sea chest comes ashore on the shingle after a gale, with a single leaf of English verse in it about a storm: who it is that drives the wave and shakes the halls.
easter_eggs.source: unlocks_793.json text.exeter_03_storm_sky (found at Dofras, 868-1066); riddles_793.json, the set exeter_storm.

easter_eggs.text: In King Edward's time ask Godric what a king's messenger pays to cross. Three pennies for his horse in winter and two in summer; the town finds the steersman and one man, and if the messenger wants more hands he hires them himself.
easter_eggs.source: Domesday Book, Dover, in Hasted's translation (History of Kent vol. 9, 1800).

unlocks.what: A place on the shingle and Wulfric's rollers
unlocks.how: Beach at Dofras three times and pay for the haul each time without being asked, or carry a message between Wulfric and his sister at Quentovic.
unlocks.gives: At Dofras act:hire_porters costs nothing and the boat is hauled above the weed line (no damage lying ashore in a gale); Wulfric tells you the turn of the stream before you set a course (the crossing to the Frankish shore is 'sure' in fair weather).

unlocks.how: End the story dofras.pilgrims_bundle with the cloaks declared (flag dofras_bundle_declared), or bring her the Frankish length from Lundenwic or Quentovic.
unlocks.gives: act:commission at the weaving huts: wool_cloth at the loom's price, cut to the length the Franks ask, ready on your next call; the cloth sells at Quentovic without a quarrel about the length.

unlocks.what: Saint Martin's half of the toll forgiven
unlocks.how: End the story dofras.archbishops_chest by carrying the chest over (flag dofras_chest_carried), or pay for the work dofras.work.church_rebuilt.
unlocks.gives: The house pays half toll at Dofras (the king's half only) for as long as there are canons; in the engine's verbs, toll at half for port.id = dofras.

unlocks.what: A burgess of Dofras, quit of toll through all England
unlocks.how: From 1042: hold the plot (dofras.work.plot), live on it a year and a day or leave a factor there, pay the king's custom, and give a man to the town's ships when they are called out. The story dofras.own_doors can give it at once.
unlocks.gives: No toll at any English port while King Edward's law stands (1042-1066); a seat in the burgesses' hall (act:lawsuit and act:witness there go in your favour as 'likely'). It ends with the fire of 1066.

unlocks.what: The carrying of the king's messengers
unlocks.how: From 1042, as a burgess or with Godric friendly: be on the strand when a messenger comes down from Canterbury.
unlocks.gives: A commission that comes again and again: one rider and his horse to the Frankish shore, 3 d in winter and 2 d in summer for the horse, and the news he carries heard a crossing before anyone else has it.

unlocks.what: The watchers of the east height
unlocks.how: End the story dofras.dead_light with the fire lit (flag dofras_fire_lit) or the song kept (flag dofras_song_kept).
unlocks.gives: act:ask_harbour at the height tells the sails seen in the strait that day and the next day's wind; a fleet passing the strait is known to you before you leave the shingle.

unlocks.what: The Wantsum, the sheltered way inside Thanet to the Thames (the shared unlock)
unlocks.how: As unlocks_793.json has it: hire the local pilot on three calls, or sail it three times. At Dofras the men of the strand will teach it over a winter to a house that holds a plot here.
unlocks.gives: As unlocks_793.json: no pilot's fee on that water and the grounding check passed as 'sure'.

unlocks.what: The Seafarer, told entire (the shared unlock)
unlocks.how: An evening's ale for Lulla at Beornflæd's house, or, after his day, for whichever old steersman has the bench by the hearth.
unlocks.gives: As unlocks_793.json: the text in the chest; told at sea it lifts the crew's heart.
